summary: This experimental RFC updates the Receiver RLOC field of the PIM Join/Prune attribute to build multicast distribution trees when source and receivers sit in different LISP sites linked by underlay IP multicast.

eli5.summary: When groups in different places want the same broadcast, routers need to know which doors lead to them. This adjusts a field so that can work across LISP sites.

questions: what is the pim receiver rloc attribute
how does lisp use underlay multicast
what does rfc 9798 change in rfc 8059
subtitle: Lets a PIM Join carry a multicast receiver address so LISP sites can share trees built on underlay multicast.

tldr.problem: RFC 8059's Receiver RLOC attribute only covered unicast-encapsulated flows (ingress replication), but LISP deployments may use IP multicast in the underlay.
tldr.mechanism: The Receiver RLOC field is redefined so it can hold a unicast or a multicast address. A multicast address may be used only when the underlay of the LISP core supports IP multicast transport.
tldr.outcome: ITRs can build underlay multicast trees for (root-RLOC, G) and map overlay groups to underlay groups flexibly. It is an Experimental RFC that updates RFC 8059.

today: RFC 9798 was published in June 2025 as an Experimental RFC and updates RFC 8059. It has not been obsoleted or updated according to the metadata.

sections.title: The Problem
sections.content:
RFC 6831 defines how multicast trees are built when the root and receivers are in different LISP sites: (EID, G) data packets are LISP-encapsulated into (RLOC, G) multicast packets. RFC 8059 defines PIM Join/Prune attributes for building these trees.

The Receiver RLOC attribute in RFC 8059 addresses only the Ingress Replication case. This document extends its scope to scenarios where the underlay uses multicast transport, consistent with the PIM Join attribute format in RFC 5384.
sections.eli5: The old rule only let a receiver name one specific address. This adds the option to name a shared group address too.

sections.title: Overlay to Underlay Group Mappings
sections.content:
When the underlay uses IP multicast, mapping the overlay group address to an underlay group address is a key engineering decision. The RFC lists three mappings:

  • Many-to-one: many (root-EID, G) flows map to a single underlay (root-RLOC, G-u) flow.
  • One-to-many: one overlay flow maps to two or more underlay flows to suit downstream xTRs.
  • One-to-one: every (root-EID, G) flow maps to its own (root-RLOC, G-u) flow.

Different subsets of xTRs may be constrained to different underlay ranges. Examples given are inter-site Proxy Tunnel Routers, which may use different ranges inside a site and in the external LISP core, and hardware resource limits on some platforms.
sections.eli5: Several shows can share one channel, one show can be sent on several channels, or each show can get its own channel.

sections.title: The Updated Receiver RLOC Field
sections.content:
Nothing changes in the syntax or semantics of the Transport Attribute, and the update applies only when its Transport field is zero (multicast). The definition of the Receiver RLOC field of the Receiver ETR RLOC attribute is changed from 'the RLOC address on which the receiver ETR wishes to receive the unicast-encapsulated flow' to the address for the encapsulated flow.

A unicast address is used for unicast-encapsulated flows, and a multicast address for multicast-encapsulated flows. A multicast address MUST be used only when the underlay of the LISP core supports IP multicast transport. Other fields are unchanged. To track the ETRs from which joins arrive, the ITR MUST use the source IP address of the incoming PIM Join/Prune, which MUST be an ETR RLOC address.
sections.eli5: The 'where should I send it' field can now hold either one person's address or a group address, as long as the network supports groups.

sections.title: How ETRs and ITRs Use It
sections.content:
An ETR that chooses the multicast underlay picks an underlay multicast group it can join (a local decision outside this document), identifies the upstream LISP site where the tree must be rooted, and builds the PIM Join/Prune as in RFC 8059, encoding only the Receiver RLOC attribute as above.

When an ITR receives the join, it allocates a new entry in the outgoing interface list for every unique underlay multicast mapping. It MAY apply local policy to rate-limit the number of underlay copies it makes.
sections.eli5: The receiver picks a channel and asks to join. The sender adds one outgoing path for each different channel asked for.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
An attacker could send numerous PIM Joins with different group addresses. This could interfere with legitimate multicast traffic if group addresses overlap, and requests to replicate for many groups could exhaust resources.

The RFC suggests PIM authentication (RFC 5796), explicit tracking of joins, and configurable limits on the number of groups per ETR RLOC used as the source of overlay joins. It has no IANA actions.
sections.eli5: A troublemaker could ask to join tons of channels. Checking who is asking and capping how many each can request helps.
